title: Sävelten sillalla – Sibelius-Akatemia vierailee
content:
Aika: lauantaina 21. marraskuuta 2026 klo 15–16:30
Paikka: Suomen Tukholman-instituutti, Snickarbacken 4
Liput: Ilmainen sisäänpääsy, mutta ilmoittaudu mielellään etukäteen tämän linkin kautta.

Lähde musiikilliselle matkalle Suomen ja Ruotsin välille! Konsertti Sävelten sillalla tarkastelee, kuinka suomalainen runous on inspiroinut ruotsalaisia ja muita pohjoismaisia säveltäjiä sekä kuinka Suomen merkittävimmät säveltäjät ovat luoneet musiikkia ruotsinkieliseen lyriikkaan niin Suomessa kuin Ruotsissakin. Helsingin Sibelius-Akatemian opiskelijat ja opettajat vierailevat Suomen instituutissa esittäen eri aikakausien lauluja monipuolisessa ja tyylillisesti rikkaassa ohjelmassa.

Konsertissa kuullaan kaikkea ikiaikaisista koraaleista ja varhaisista tienraivaajista, kuten Bernhard Henrik Crusellista, kansallisromantiikan rakastettuihin klassikoihin kuten Jean Sibeliukseen, Armas Järnefeltiin ja Selim Palmgreniin. Illan ohjelmassa on myös nykymusiikkia Carita Holmströmiltä ja Sebastian Fagerlundilta.

Konsertin aikana musiikkia ja ohjelmiston taustoja avaa Gustav Djupsjöbacka keskustelussa Suomen instituutin johtajan Wivan Nygård-Fageruddin kanssa.

title: SLS finansierar forskning om språkhat, aktivt åldrande och medicinska recept från 1700-talet
content:
Svenska litteratursällskapet beviljar sammanlagt närmare 2,4 miljoner euro till fyra forskningsprojekt inom socialvetenskaper, historia och hälsovetenskap.

SLS vetenskapliga råd har beviljat forskningsmedel till följande projekt:

Språkhat: Stereotyper och affekt i språkrelationer tar sin utgångspunkt i den paradox att svenska i Finland samtidigt är ett nationalspråk och ett återkommande mål för fientlig retorik och ifrågasättande. Forskarna jämför hur svenska framställts i media och inom politiken under det första decenniet av Finlands självständighet (1917–1927) med en period i den digitala eran (2007–2027). Vilka olika uttryck har språkhatet tagit och vilka är likheterna och skillnaderna mellan framställningarna för hundra år sedan och i dag? Projektet leds av professor Tuija Saresma vid Östra Finlands universitet.

title: Europe vs. Elon: 5 ways the EU is trying to squeeze out Musk’s Starlink
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Union is fighting Elon Musk’s Starlink on at least five fronts —from blocking access, to boosting rivals, to drafting new rules aimed directly at undermining the tech mogul’s growing dominance over the space business.

The world’s richest man is expanding his grip on space and looking to turn his satellite broadband champion Starlink into a “major mobile carrier.” The recent news that the system’s military-grade service in Ukraine was slowed down, hampering Kyiv’s defenses against Russian attacks, exposed — yet again — the risks of relying on one man’s business during wartime.

In Europe, governments and companies fear the reliance on Musk’s technology — and they’re ramping up their efforts to push back.

“Ukraine’s dependence on Starlink highlights the vulnerability of European defense systems that rely on U.S. technology,” center-right Finnish member of the European Parliament Aura Salla said in a statement. It’s “another reminder that Europe must reduce its dangerous technological dependencies — ASAP.”

POLITICO breaks down five ways the European Union is trying to crack down on the dominance of Musk’s satellites in our skies.

title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
content:
Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.

The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across Serbian society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and creeping authoritarianism of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.

In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the Pledge EU Horizon project. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.

title: The upside of untidiness: why a little mess can be good for your home
content:
If we’re to follow the philosophy of organiser extraordinaire Marie Kondo, a tidy home is a better home.

Albert Einstein, however, might have contested that point. “If a cluttered desk is a sign of a cluttered mind,” goes a quote widely attributed to the famed physicist, “of what, then, is an empty desk a sign?”

My newly published research, which studied 22 New Zealand households, also challenges the conventional wisdom that mess is a problem which must be fixed.

Far from being a symptom of poor organisation, mess can help families function and make life run more smoothly.

Consider the spaces in our homes that serve more than one purpose, and where things tend to pile up. A living room that doubles as a play area, or a bedroom that also serves as a study.

One couple told me how their dining table becomes a “drop zone” for belongings such as bags and drink bottles, before it’s cleared each evening. Another person described how leaving something on his kitchen island made him less likely to forget it when leaving the house.

title: Op-ed | What the US Midterms Could Mean for American Foreign Policy
content:
On 3 November, the United States (US) will hold midterm elections. Polls point towards a result which will change the balance of power in Washington, with the Democratic Party predicted to take control of the House of Representatives and quite possibly the Senate. Even just a Democratic victory in the House – the lower chamber of Congress – could have implications for American foreign policy.

These implications could push in two contradictory directions. On the one hand, Congress has some powers which are relevant to US foreign policy. The Senate – the upper house of Congress – must give its consent to treaties and ambassadorial appointments. Congress as a whole must approve the budget for the US military and for the country’s diplomatic agencies. It also has the power to investigate and hold to account officials who engage in corrupt or lawless behaviour. All of this suggests that a Democratic Congress could impose meaningful restraints on President Donald Trump.

content:

Presidentti Donald Trumpin yritys kontrolloida amerikkalaisen kulttuurin narratiivia kulttuuriorganisaatioiden kautta heijastelee maan demokratian rapautumista sekä muistuttaa, miksi taide on autoritäärisen johtajan pahin vihollinen. 

Kylmän sodan aikana Washington, D.C.:ssä presidentti Dwight D. title: Some of the Spookiest Specters in the Library’s Archives
content:
What’s the scariest part of working at a library? The ghost writers.  

Library staffers aren’t easily spooked — as proved by a recent presentation on some of the collection’s most haunting finds, just in time for Halloween. 

In the Prints and Photographs Division, spirit photography in the 19th century reflected how grief and loss fueled a spiritualism phase in the 1850s and 1860s, explained archivist Maggie McCready. The massive loss of life during the Civil War, combined with Victorian anxiety about death, led to a desire to connect with deceased loved ones.  

Enter photographers such as William H. Mumler, who claimed to show spirits in their images. The reality? Using old glass plate negatives left a ghostly image behind on the new photograph.  

Scandal struck when it turned out that one of the “spirits” in a Mumler photo was, in fact, alive. A few years later, in 1869, New York authorities ran a sting operation and arrested Mumler for fraud. The prosecution’s star witness was P. T. Barnum (not known for his adherence to the truth), who was photographed in a phony spirit image featuring Abraham Lincoln.

title: The UAE has so much blood on its hands in Sudan. For its nominee to lead the UN would be an outrage | Nesrine Malik
content:
Lana Nusseibeh has been the face of a disastrous Emirates policy that has prolonged war and death. It is a scandal that she is even being considered

Over the past few years, you can plot the plunge into global instability not only through the unchecked assaults on international law and civilian life, but through the decline and undermining of the authority and credibility of international institutions. The latest level in this spiral is the proposed appointment of Lana Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as the UN secretary general. Her bid has been rapidly gaining momentum and endorsements. And it has been met with outrage among the Sudanese.

Nusseibeh is the minister of state at the UAE and a former UAE ambassador to the UN. For the past three years, the country has been connected to – bear with me, this will be a long sentence – supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia in Sudan, facilitating mercenaries to fight alongside the militia (which is accused of ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity and sexual violence), and appropriating international aid infrastructure to smuggle weapons into the country.

title: THL ja Sydänliitto ehdottavat elintarvikkeiden terveysveroa – suolan käyttö ei ole vähentynyt
content:
Kansallisten ravitsemussuositusten mukaan suolaa tulisi saada enintään viisi grammaa vuorokaudessa. THL:n tiedotteen mukaan lähes kaikilla työikäisillä raja ylittyy. Äskettäin julkaistun tutkimuksen mukaan työikäisten miesten suolan saanti oli vuonna 2023 keskimäärin 10,3 grammaa ja naisten 7,6 grammaa vuorokaudessa. Saanti oli samalla tasolla kuin vuonna 2017.

Suurin osa ruokavalion suolasta tulee viljavalmisteista, kuten leivistä, lihavalmisteista, kuten makkaroista, sekä juustoista ja valmisaterioista. Liiallinen suolan saanti nostaa verenpainetta ja kuormittaa pitkällä aikavälillä myös munuaisia.

Suomalaisten verenpaine laski vuosikymmenten ajan 2000-luvun alkuun asti, mutta kehitys on sittemmin tasaantunut. Vuonna 2023 työikäisistä miehistä 43 prosentilla ja naisista 32 prosentilla verenpaine oli koholla tai heillä oli verenpainelääkitys. Verenpaineen hallinta on keskeistä sydän- ja verisuonitautien ehkäisyssä, ja nämä sairaudet ovat Suomen yleisin kuolinsyy.

“Suolan saannin vähentäminen on väestötasolla tutkitusti tehokas keino ehkäistä kohonnutta verenpainetta”, sanoo THL:n erikoistutkija Niina Kaartinen.

title: What Should the Rules for A.I. Companies Actually Be? We Asked the Experts.
content:
What should the government do? We asked a panel of experts to assess the risks A.I. presents and the tools of governance that could be adopted to address them.

Kate Brennan, a former Google tech worker, leads the policy agenda on A.I. and corporate power at the AI Now Institute, an independent research institute providing expert analysis on A.I. in the public interest.

Brennan: Here’s what I see as the biggest risk: These companies are spending so much money on building out this technology. The consulting firm Bain estimates that by 2031, they will have to achieve $6 trillion of revenue annually to sustain their current level of capital expenditure, which is $1.5 trillion a year. In order for those numbers to add up in any way, they need to push this tech everywhere, into all of our public institutions and contracting, including in areas where A.I. is not fit for purpose, is not secure, safe by design. That’s what we should be talking about.

Brennan: Government is supposed to stop harmful products from entering the market. We do it with drugs. We do it with airplanes. The issue here is corporate negligence. That should be the focus.

title: I See You, ICC
content: The International Criminal Court (ICC) won the EU's human rights prize last week, a big vote of support from the European Parliament for its work in putting war criminals on trial and just 13 days after the US imposed sanctions on the tribunal. But it's “somewhat problematic” for the EU's assembly to award the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought to the court “whilst simultaneously being indecisive and arguably weak regarding its responses to the US sanctions,” said Benjamin Thorne, an assistant law professor at the University of Reading. The Hague-based court, backed by 125 countries, has convicted 15 people to date, all from African countries. It currently has arrest warrants for Russian president Vladimir Putin and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. title: In Leaked Audio, Flock CEO Tells Cops Backlash to the Company Isn’t Real
content:
Garrett Langley, the CEO of automatic license plate reader company Flock, told an audience of police chiefs at a private police conference Sunday that anti-Flock protests around the country are not real, according to leaked audio obtained by 404 Media.

He also said his wife advised him to never apologize, said he would prefer to never do interviews with the press again, and claimed without evidence that the social media opposition to Flock is driven mostly by Russian bots.

“Somebody was paying for [the social media posts and] stopped paying for it,” Langley said about the many viral posts criticizing his company’s technology. “Social media chatter on Flock is down about 95 percent from July. It went down 50 percent last week when Ukraine bombed a Russian data center with a drone. Literally 50 percent overnight. And so look, I’m the last person, my wife as well, she’s like ‘This is crazy, these people are getting paid to say these things,’” he added, repeating a disproven theory that Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers had a significant impact on internet bot activity.

title: Russia: Exiled advocate faces “extremism” charges over human rights work for Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO Memorial
content:
Reacting to news that a prosecutor’s office in Moscow is about to initiate criminal proceedings on “extremism” charges against prisoners’ rights advocate Anna Karetnikova, from the Memorial Human Rights Centre, who is currently living in exile, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:

“Amnesty International has long warned of the danger that Russia’s vague and overly broad anti-extremism legislation would be used to criminalize lawful human rights work. Today, those fears are being realized with the criminal case against Anna Karetnikova – the first time such charges have been used against an individual solely because of their human rights work.”

“Although Anna Karetnikova is living in exile and can only be tried in absentia, the threat of prosecution sends a chilling message that is intended to silence human defenders in Russia and abroad, stop them from documenting violations and deter them from speaking up for the victims of these abuses. Criminalizing the human rights work of a leading, Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO is a harmful and shameful move that further exposes Russian authorities’ true motives.

title: Serbia's Student-Led Movement Ousts Strongman Aleksander Vučić in Shock Election Result
content:
Serbia’s longtime leader Aleksander Vučić has been swept out of power by a historic student-led opposition movement against Vučić’s right-wing Serbian Progressive Party. Candidates from the Student List, who are not students themselves but largely first-time politicians selected by student-led popular assemblies, won a majority of seats in Sunday’s parliamentary elections, marking a seismic shift in Serbian politics. Their victory comes two years into a student-led movement sparked by the collapse of a roof at a train station in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 people. The disaster became a focal point for anti-government protests over corruption, cronyism, political violence and democratic backsliding.

“Students really changed the whole political landscape of the country, and maybe even more important, they changed political imagination. They changed our understanding of what’s politically possible for all of us,” says journalist Lela Vujanić, who speaks to us from Belgrade about the groundbreaking elections. “This was a great democratic opening and democratic awakening, not only for the students, but for the rest of the country also.”

content:
The vast amount of information on the open web requires researchers and journalists to adapt with new tools to make sense of it all. Checking facts, gauging public opinion, and other lines of inquiry depend on being able to analyze the overwhelming amount of material posted online every day. Unfortunately, responding to the AI industry’s voracious appetite for data, companies stewarding this public data are looking to cash in and block access to the open web. This makes the web harder to navigate, and threatens all kinds of important research.

Reddit’s lawsuit against SerpAPI[1] and Perplexity threatens to do exactly that.

Reddit was once a very open platform, fostering a community of alternative apps and extensions putting users in control of their experience. Since the rise of AI however, it changed tack. Over the last three years Reddit has closed APIs to users, limited UI features, and otherwise restrained access without login. By making the voices on the platform harder to access, the company has positioned itself as a gatekeeper, and has since struck a lucrative data-sharing arrangement with Google.

title: Vote young yet govern much later: West African youth’s struggle for power
content:
In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely

Originally published on Global Voices

Youth mobilized in Africa. Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel

In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18. In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25. However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50  years old before being eligible to run for the highest office. Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.

Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves. The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?

title: Sudan: One Year on from the Cataclysm of El Fasher
content:
“It is as if a tsunami had hit the city,” said a resident who returned to Sudan’s El Fasher only to find it destroyed and largely abandoned after the Rapid Support Forces’ (RSF) October 2025 takeover.

For 18 months, the RSF laid siege to the city, digging a trench around it in its final months, forcing starving residents to survive on animal fodder, until even that ran out. 

In the siege’s final weeks, the RSF increasingly used drones to target government soldiers, aligned armed groups, and civilians who were ensnared in a tiny area, leaving many maimed or dead. 

During the last days of the offensive, the RSF committed multiple massacres. The UN Human Rights Office estimates over 6,000 people were killed in just three days.

RSF fighters also committed widespread sexual violence against women and girls and ran a massive abduction-for-ransom racket, killing those who couldn’t pay. Thousands of civilians may still languish in RSF dungeons. 

Colombian private military contractors trained in UAE military bases were deployed alongside the RSF on the front lines, operating drones and artillery. Survivors’ accounts confirm the contractors were present during some of the worst atrocities.

title: Hear an Hour of the Jazzy Background Music from the Original 1967 Spider-Man Cartoon
content:
Ray Ellis had a six-decade career as a producer, arranger, and jazz composer. And while he’s best known for arranging music for Billie Holiday’s Lady in Satin (1958), he also enjoyed a long career orchestrating music for television. Working under a pseudonym “Yvette Blais” (his wife’s name), Ellis composed background music for the cartoon studio Filmation between 1968 and 1982. And, during the late 60s, he notably created the background and incidental music for the original Spider-Man cartoons.

Above, hear Ray Ellis’ Spider-Man soundtrack. The show’s talking parts and sound effects have been removed as much as possible, then “pieced back together into complete form,” by a YouTuber who uses the moniker “11db11.” All of the music from Season 1 is included, plus many recordings from Seasons 2 and 3. It’s worth noting that the 52 episodes from the original 1967 Spider-Man TV series have been completely restored. You can purchase them on DVD online.

title: Cybersecurity CEO Indicted for Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims
content:
A Florida man who was the subject of a 2019 investigation by ProPublica was indicted last month on federal charges that he defrauded clients of his ransomware data recovery firm. 

According to the Justice Department, the man, Zohar Pinhasi, told customers he could recover their encrypted files without having to pay hackers, when, in reality, he paid the ransom and charged victims a hefty fee on top.

The indictment mirrors the findings from ProPublica’s 2019 article “The Trade Secret,” which centered on Pinhasi and his scheme. The outlet found that the ransomware victims were being harmed twice: once by the hackers, who locked their targets’ files and demanded ransom, and a second time by MonsterCloud, Pinhasi’s Florida-based data recovery firm, which misled its clients about not paying ransoms.

“By falsely claiming to decrypt ransomware without paying off the ransomers, the defendant re-victimized his clients while extracting a hefty profit for himself,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in an Oct. 7 press release. “Our Office will vigorously prosecute ransomware attackers who prey on Americans from across the world and those who cynically profit from their criminal activity.”

title: Where did bats come from? New research points to Europe
content:
For decades scientists have argued about where bats originated. A recently published study in the journal Nature offers new evidence to address that question. This new international study combining DNA and fossils supports Europe as bats’ likely birthplace.

The problem thus far has been that, unlike birds, which have a superb fossil record showing the transition from dinosaur to “chicken”, when we find bat fossils, they are exquisitely near-fully formed “bats”.

Bats are the only mammals capable of powered flight. Earlier reconstructions suggested the US, Africa or Asia as bats’ birthplace, with different datasets and models producing different answers. The oldest known bat skeletons, discovered in Wyoming in the US, date to the early Eocene geological epoch, about 52 million years ago. Their elongated wing fingers show that bats could already fly.

However, the location of the oldest known fossils does not necessarily reveal where a group first evolved. These fossils nevertheless provide important clues about early bat anatomy, relationships and distributions. What is missing is a fossil sequence documenting the transition from non-flying ancestors to the earliest flying bats.

title: Lapin sodan jäljet näkyvät yhä ihmisten elämässä
content:
Sotien historiaa on perinteisesti tarkasteltu taisteluiden, joukkojen liikkeiden ja poliittisten tapahtumien kautta. Uusi kokemushistoriallista tutkimusta hyödyntävä artikkelikokoelma selvittää, miltä sota tuntui ihmisistä, miten poikkeusoloissa selvittiin ja millaisia pitkäaikaisia vaikutuksia kokemuksilla oli yksilöille, perheille ja yhteisöille.

”Lapin sota ei loppunut ihmisten elämässä siihen, kun viimeiset saksalaiset sotilaat poistuivat Suomesta. Ihmiset palasivat tuhotuille kotiseuduille ja rakensivat elämänsä uudelleen", sanoo yliopistotutkija Outi Autti Oulun yliopiston tiedotteessa.

"Kokemukset kulkivat mukana vuosikymmeniä. Osa niistä kerrottiin eteenpäin, osasta vaiettiin. Sodan jälkiä voi nähdä vielä seuraavissa sukupolvissa", Autti muistuttaa.

Tutkimus nostaa esiin erityisesti evakkouden merkityksen. Kymmenettuhannet lappilaiset joutuivat jättämään kotinsa ja aloittamaan elämänsä uudelleen sodan jälkeen.

”Kokemukset vaihtelivat suuresti riippuen iästä, sukupuolesta, asuinpaikasta, kielestä ja siitä, minne evakkomatka vei. Myös mahdollisuudet selviytyä ja rakentaa elämää uudelleen olivat erilaisia”, Autti kertoo.

title: Död ved och levande urskog – möt Per Törevall, vinnare av Wiki Loves Earth 2026
content:
En fallen torrfura i Pellokielas urskog i Norrbotten tog hem förstaplatsen i årets svenska Wiki Loves Earth. Vi har pratat med fotografen Per Törevall om bilden, skogen och varför han ville vara med i tävlingen.

I augusti presenterade vi vinnarna i Wiki Loves Earth 2026. I år deltog 60 fotografer, som tillsammans laddade upp 1 266 bilder från skyddad natur runt om i Sverige. Förstaplatsen gick till Per Törevall, som deltog under användarnamnet Bilparadiset15, för en bild från Pellokielas urskog i Norrbottens län.

Per tog bilden i början av oktober 2020. Den visar en gles, gammal skog där en torrfura har fallit. Runt den står levande tallar som har blivit mycket gamla, med inslag av björk.

– Jag vill gärna fotografera den här typen av skog eftersom den ser så speciell ut, säger Per Törevall.

Per valde höjd och vinkel så att den som tittar på bilden ska få känslan av att stå mitt i skogen. Juryn lyfte fram hur bilden visar att även ett dött träd kan vara en central del av ett levande ekosystem, och hur kompositionen och det naturliga ljuset förmedlar skogens ålder.

title: Man up, don't save the planet
content: Are you a man who cares about the climate? Then you might be a “soy boy” (or for our less chronically online readers: lacking masculine traits). Research suggests that men who want to protect the environment are often seen as warmer and more caring – traits traditionally associated with femininity. Michael Haselhuhn, an associate professor of management at the University of California, published research on this. When asked if they would use cold water for laundry to save money, most men said they would. “When I said it helps the environment because it saves electricity, the support dropped by 10%,” Haselhuhn said. Across most European countries, there is a gender gap in how women and men see environmental issues. title: Brazil: Lula Wins Stunning Upset Over Flávio Bolsonaro in Blow to Far Right & Trump
content:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a record fourth term in office, defeating far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro by 4 million votes in a runoff election on Sunday. Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who remains under house arrest for plotting a coup against Lula four years ago. The younger Bolsonaro, who narrowly defeated Lula in the first round of voting earlier this month, is now refusing to concede.

Lula’s surprise comeback comes after weeks of student-led organizing and campaigning on his behalf, and amid accusations that U.S.-based tech companies were suppressing Lula’s reach online in favor of his Trump-aligned opponent. “The amount of organizing, the amount of marches and rallies, campaigning, pamphlets that we’ve seen the last three weeks has been something that I have never seen in my entire life, ever, covering elections for decades in so many different countries. It is absolutely unprecedented,” says Brazil-based journalist Michael Fox. “It is an absolute game-changer for the region.”

title: Hungarian Tycoon’s Firm Funded Pro-Orbán Advertising Agency, Records Show
content:
A firm owned by Hungarian construction mogul László Szíjj — who amassed a fortune under previous Prime Minister Viktor Orbán — donated about $863,000 to Megafon, a political advertising agency that promoted the former ruling party. 

The donations are detailed in two years of annual financial statements from Szíjj’s firm, Vakond Via Kft., which were examined by OCCRP and Direkt36. The company made “cash grants” that totaled 300 million Hungarian forints to Megafon Digital Incubator Center, adding up to about $252,000 in 2024, and $611,000 the following year.

Launched in 2020, Megafon became one of Hungary’s most influential political advertising agencies, mainly running social media campaigns in support of Orbán’s Fidesz party.

But since Orbán’s stunning electoral defeat in April, after 16-years in power, Megafon has kept a low profile. The company’s website was taken offline in August, and its employees have fallen from 72 to three, according to information from a firm that provides commercial registry data.

Neither Megafon nor Szíjj responded to requests for comment.

title: Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track
content:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

title: Turun AMK perustaa uuden tutkimus- ja osaamiskeskuksen meriteollisuuden tarpeisiin

Uusi Meri- ja laivanrakennusteknologian keskus kokoaa Turun ammattikorkeakoulun meriteollisuutta palvelevan tutkimuksen ja koulutuksen yhteen. Keskus vahvistaa Turun ammattikorkeakoulun roolia meriteollisuuden osaamisen ja uusien teknologioiden kehittäjänä.

title: Coffeemaxxed lifestyle
content: As a coffee addict, I dream of living in a city where cafés stay open for as much of the day as possible, ideally opening early and closing late. But my past geographical choices haven’t exactly served me well. To find out where I should have settled, I collected Google Maps listings for cafés in about 80 of Europe’s largest cities, covering roughly 15,000 active cafés. The data revealed a few interesting things beyond opening hours. London and Istanbul have the most café listings, but neither scores particularly well in customer reviews. If you’re after the best-rated cafés, Romania is a good choice: Bucharest’s cafés have a median rating of 4.8 out of 5, based on more than 30,000 reviews. Still, Bucharest wouldn’t satisfy me: its cafés stay open for about 10 hours a day. That’s much better than Leeds, where cafés are open for just seven hours on average. For a coffee fanatic like me, the Balkans and Istanbul may be the best bet: cafés in Tirana, Podgorica, Zagreb and Pristina stay open for around 15 hours a day. title: SLS finansierar forskning om språkhat, aktivt åldrande och medicinska recept från 1700-talet
content:
Svenska litteratursällskapet beviljar sammanlagt närmare 2,4 miljoner euro till fyra forskningsprojekt inom socialvetenskaper, historia och hälsovetenskap.

SLS vetenskapliga råd har beviljat forskningsmedel till följande projekt:

Språkhat: Stereotyper och affekt i språkrelationer tar sin utgångspunkt i den paradox att svenska i Finland samtidigt är ett nationalspråk och ett återkommande mål för fientlig retorik och ifrågasättande. Forskarna jämför hur svenska framställts i media och inom politiken under det första decenniet av Finlands självständighet (1917–1927) med en period i den digitala eran (2007–2027). Vilka olika uttryck har språkhatet tagit och vilka är likheterna och skillnaderna mellan framställningarna för hundra år sedan och i dag? Projektet leds av professor Tuija Saresma vid Östra Finlands universitet.

title: ChatGPT Keeps Telling People 404 Media Can Solve Their Tech Support Problems
content:
Last week, I got an email from a man in Russia whose Instagram account had been banned. “I have now lost access to 13 years of personal photos, videos and memories,” he wrote. “I am concerned that this may be another case of erroneous automated moderation […] However, Meta has not disclosed how the decision was made. Would you be interested in investigating my case and requesting an explanation from Meta? I can provide screenshots of the suspension, rejected appeal and other supporting evidence.”

The email seemed AI-generated, like many others we have gotten recently. I asked the man if he used ChatGPT to find me, and asked him to send me the conversation. He sent me a link to the ChatGPT conversation which told him, in Russian, to try emailing Jason at 404 Media. 

“How can I get my account back?” the man asked ChatGPT on Wednesday. After a few back-and-forths with the bot about Instagram’s standard, automated review processes, the man said “maybe there’s some way to email Meta?” ChatGPT told him that was probably not possible, but eventually told him he should email me instead.

title: SLS rahoittaa kielivihaan, aktiiviseen ikääntymiseen ja 1700-luvun lääkeresepteihin liittyvää tutkimusta
content:
Svenska litteratursällskapet (SLS) myöntää yhteensä lähes 2,4 miljoonaa euroa neljälle tutkimushankkeelle. Hankkeet liittyvät yhteiskuntatieteisiin, historiantutkimukseen ja terveystieteisiin.

SLS:n tieteellinen johtokunta on päättänyt myöntää tutkimusrahoitusta seuraaville hankkeille:

Kieliviha: stereotypiat ja affektit kielisuhteissa–hankkeen lähtökohtana on paradoksi, jossa ruotsin kieli on Suomessa samanaikaisesti sekä kansalliskieli että toistuvan vihamielisen retoriikan ja kyseenalaistamisen kohde. Tutkijat vertailevat, miten ruotsin kieltä on kuvattu mediassa ja politiikassa Suomen itsenäisyyden ensimmäisellä vuosikymmenellä (1917–1927) ja digitalisoituneella aikakaudella (2007–2027). Minkälaisia eri muotoja kieliviha on saanut? Mitä eroja ja yhteneväisyyksiä sadan vuoden takaisissa ja nykyisissä kuvauksissa on? Hanketta johtaa Itä-Suomen yliopiston professori Tuija Saresma.

title: CMI co-organises Nordic peace mediation seminar during Nordic Council Session
content:
CMI co-organises a seminar on Nordic peace mediation at the Parliament of Finland in Helsinki on 26 October. Held in conjunction with the 78th Session of the Nordic Council, ‘Nordic peace mediation in a changing world order’ will examine opportunities for closer Nordic cooperation in peace mediation amid a changing geopolitical environment.

Organised by the Finnish delegation to the Nordic Council and CMI, the side-event brings together Nordic Council parliamentarians, political leaders and peace mediation experts to discuss how the Nordic countries can strengthen their collective contribution to international peace and stability.

The seminar can be watched live from 13.00–13.50 with a recording available on the website of the Nordic Council. Panellists are expected to speak in their own Nordic language.

Monday’s discussion takes place against a backdrop of intensified power politics, growing strategic competition and increasing pressure on the rules-based international order. These developments have changed the international environment for peace mediation and challenged the capacity of traditional multilateral institutions to address conflicts.

title: Between two shores: The ‘Monhés,’ nationality, and a sense of belonging in Mozambique
content:
Being Mozambican is a matter of belonging — regardless of one’s origin, appearance, or surname

Originally published on Global Voices

Indians in Mozambique celebrating the Hindu festival of Navratri. Image by Kash_if via Flickr. CC BY 2.0.

In Mozambique, the word monhé has a much deeper history than its everyday use might suggest. Depending on who says it and the context, it can simply be a reference to the population of Indian origin, an identity marker, or a prejudiced remark. But behind the word there is a history of migration, trade, colonialism, independence, displacement, and, above all, belonging.

The question of who is Mozambican gets particularly interesting when we look at the communities of Indian origin, who have lived in the country for several generations. Are they Mozambicans? Indians? Foreigners? Or, in some cases, stateless persons? The answer cannot be found in appearance, surname, religion, or family origin alone. It is found in the country’s history and, particularly, in its nationality law.

Being Mozambican is a matter of belonging — regardless of one’s origin, appearance, or surname

title: Sri Lanka Records Zero Prosecutions Amid Online Scam Surge
content:
Authorities in Sri Lanka have failed to successfully prosecute a single transnational cyber scam case, police have said, despite more than a thousand arrests so far this year of suspected members of Asian fraud syndicates who have surged into the South Asian country.

The admission comes as experts warn the island nation is becoming a destination of choice for thousands of scam workers fleeing Southeast Asian nations such as Cambodia, which had in recent years become home to massive scam compounds, many of them reliant on trafficked workers.

Recently crackdowns in scam centers in Southeast Asia have driven mostly Chinese-origin scam syndicates to set up shop in vulnerable states from Madagascar to Papua New Guinea.
Among the countries of South Asia, Sri Lanka stands out for being at “serious risk of becoming a hub for industrial-scale cyber scams,” the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) said last month.

From January until September, Sri Lankan police have conducted raids on 27 suspected scam compounds around the country and arrested 1093 people, Sri Lankan police spokesman Fredrick Wootler told OCCRP and Sri Lanka’s The Sunday Times.

title: A Texas Cop Signed on to Help ICE Deport His Neighbors. It Tore the Town Apart.
content:
The new patrol officer parked his black Dodge Charger outside a house off Main Street and approached on foot. A Mexican ballad was playing. Someone had called in a noise complaint, claiming it sounded as if people were fighting.

But as the officer, Jaron Alexander, got closer, he found nothing of the sort. A middle-aged woman greeted him as her daughter, Joanna Martinez, petite and visibly pregnant, looked on. “What kind of party are you all having?” she remembers him asking. Behind her were three generations of an extended family. They were celebrating a 3-month-old’s baptism over pozole verde, horchata and beers.

Alexander ran some IDs and found no issues. The music wasn’t even that loud, he thought. He told them to have a good night, and then he left.

That encounter, in early October last year, was the first of many that Alexander and Martinez would have in tiny Ingram, Texas, a 1.5-square-mile town of 1,900 people beside the Guadalupe River. But it was the only one before Ingram signed an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that would roil the town and tear Martinez’s family apart.

title: Canada and Europe want to reshape the global order. But whose vision will prevail?
content:
Mark Carney’s push for a middle-powers alliance meets Ursula von der Leyen’s bid for influence.

By ZI-ANN LUM, SEBASTIAN STARCEVIC
and CAMILLE GIJS

Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO

Mark Carney’s pursuit of a global alliance of middle powers has a Europe problem.

Canada’s prime minister wants to help build a new world order that can counterbalance the power of the United States and China. But his vision depends on a new relationship with a Europe that doesn’t see itself as a middle power at all. 

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has a different vision: a Brussels-centered bloc that extends the EU’s economic and geopolitical influence, starting with Canada. The idea, according to senior European lawmaker Siegfried Mureșan, is to create an opportunity for the EU to become the “global center of gravity for liberal democracies.”

title: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders
content:
We all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious moments

Happy birthday, Lara! This month marks 30 years since Ms Croft first swan-dived into our lives with her unique blend of athletic prowess, archaeological expertise and giant knockers. More than 100 million Tomb Raider games have been sold since. We all remember the good times: the bold design and sheer playability of the original titles; the establishment of Lara as a 90s icon, embodying both lads’ mag culture and girl power; the way she made games cool, even appearing on the cover of the Face. We’ve had blockbuster movies, big budget reboots, and shiny reissues. And who could forget the time we got to powerwash her house?

But no one gets to 30 without a few skeletons in the closet – or in Lara’s case, butlers in the freezer. So here’s a look at the darker parts of her past.

title: Ukrainassa puolustusteknologiaa kehitetään rohkein harppauksin, Suomessa harkituin askelin
content:
Autonomiset järjestelmät ja kehittyvä teknologia muuttavat sodankäyntiä nopeammin kuin perinteiset puolustusorganisaatiot kykenevät mukautumaan. Ukraina on olosuhteiden pakottamana osoittanut tässä suhteessa edistyksellisyyttä testaamalla uutta puolustusteknologiaa ketterästi: matalalla kynnyksellä ja nopealla syklillä. Suomessa lähestymistapa on maltillisempi. Analyysissa syvennytään suomalaisen puolustusteknologiayritys Kova Labsin kokemuksiin Ukrainasta, jossa toimintaympäristö on teknologisen kehityksen kannalta otollinen.

Sotateknologian kehitystä ajoi toisen maailmansodan aikaan valtiojohtoinen innovaatioekosysteemi, jossa valtio rahoitti ja koordinoi teknologista kehitystä sotilaallisten tarpeiden pohjalta. 2020-luvun muuttuneessa turvallisuuspoliittisessa ympäristössä tilanne on käänteinen, sillä puolustusorganisaatioiden kehitys ei pysy siviilijohtoisen teknologisen kilpajuoksun tahdissa.

title: Queer mediums of the cult of María Lionza are redefining the gender binary in Venezuela’s sacred mountain
content:
Gender diversity, resistance and ritual cross-dressing in Venezuela's sacred cult

Originally published on Global Voices

Portrait of Wander Rodríguez, part of the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers, and the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In Venezuela, Spiritism as a religion is part of the collective imagination, of our identity; popular beliefs and ritual practices that take us back to our ancestors in colonial times. Over the years, Spiritism has evolved into a vibrant, contemporary national cult centered on the figure of María Lionza as the principal protector of waters and the charms of nature, a figure who challenges the notions of the patriarchal state and opposes monotheistic religions.

This religious system has been studied in depth by anthropologists in our country (Daisy Barreto, Angelina Pollak-Eltz, Michelle Asencio, Francisco Ferrándiz, Cesar Escalona, among others), which I had read about and found interesting at the time, but which I later witnessed for the first time in its most important sites, such as Quibayo and Sorte, in the state of Yaracuy, Venezuela.

title: Chinese Scam Boss Murdered in Sri Lanka Had Multiple Identities
content:
A Chinese cyber scam boss who was kidnapped and murdered in Sri Lanka’s capital in July went by three separate aliases and carried at least two passports, according to documents obtained by OCCRP and The Sunday Times.

Chen Guoqing, 31, was abducted from the Colombo Port City special economic zone in the early hours of July 23 by a group of over a dozen men, one of them brandishing a pistol, according to a copy of the police investigative report into the incident. He was driven to a rural area over 70 kilometers east of Colombo, tortured to death, and his body was abandoned.

The murder of Chen — and the hunt for his killers — received extensive media coverage in Sri Lanka, amid fears that the South Asian country is becoming a new base for Asian criminal syndicates that target victims around the world with sophisticated online fraud schemes.

title: An Ancient Virus Explains Why the Human Brain Is Special
content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that invaded our brains, thought fast, swapped coffins, and hit the art gallery.

First, an ancient viral pandemic that afflicted many of our primate relatives—but somehow missed humans—may help explain how we got so smart (relatively speaking). Then: mammal brains eat crow, an upcycled sarcophagus, and a trip to the starry Provençal summer of 1889.

As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files. 

Gerdes, Patricia; Karlsson, Ofelia; Garza, Raquel; Atacho, Diahann A. M. et al. “Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains.” Science Advances.

A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago shaped the divergence of human and chimp brain development, shedding light on how our own species came to be more cognitively complex than our closest living relatives, according to a new study.

title: Big Tech and authoritarian states: Belarus
content:
A Global Voices video podcast on the state of digital repression in Belarus

Originally published on Global Voices

Interviewer: Daria Dergacheva | Guest: Mikhail Doroshevich.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

There are more autocracies in the world in 2026 than there are democracies. Some researchers identify digital authoritarianism as the use of digital technology by regimes to surveil, repress, and manipulate domestic and foreign populations. Others argue that the same practices are also carried out by hybrid and democratic regimes. However, they can not execute them without major tech companies becoming complicit, with or without their knowledge.

title: Starlink connection restored at high speed in Ukraine, defense minister says
content:
SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services have been restored in Ukraine, allowing the country’s forces to operate drones at high speed, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Saturday.

“The Ministry of Defense’s monitoring systems indicate that Starlink/Starshield speeds have been restored,” Khmara told reporters in WhatsApp messages. “We are recording speeds exceeding 400 km/h, and the connection is stable.”

Since last week, Kyiv had been reporting speed limits on Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade service, affecting Ukraine’s ability to use drones and carry out defensive strikes. The throttling came amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump blaming President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the continuation of the war with Russia.

On Friday, Ukrainian officials told POLITICO that drones continued to lose signal at speeds above 160 km/h, despite U.S. President Donald Trump saying on Thursday that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had “put it back.” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham raised the issue in a phone call with Trump on Friday.

title: Lakkasiko Suomi auttamasta palestiinalaispakolaisia? Hallituksen UNRWA-päätös puntarissa
content:
Ulkopolitiikan arvot punnitaan päätöksissä. Mitä Suomen vetäytyminen UNRWAn rahoittajien joukosta tarkoittaa?

YK:n palestiinalaispakolaisjärjestö UNRWA on ajettu ahtaalle, ja Suomi on liittynyt järjestön rahoituksen lakkauttaneiden maiden joukkoon muun muassa Yhdysvaltojen ja Ruotsin rinnalla. Samaan aikaan Suomi jatkaa puolustusmateriaaliyhteistyötä Israelin kanssa, korostaa monenkeskisen järjestelmän ja kansainvälisen oikeuden kunnioittamista ulkopolitiikkansa perustana ja kampanjoi pääsystä YK:n turvallisuusneuvoston vaihtuvaksi jäseneksi.

Miten rahoituksen supistuminen näkyy UNRWAn toiminnassa, ja miten Suomen päätös vetäytyä pois rahoittajamaiden joukosta asettuu osaksi Suomen ulkopolitiikan suuria linjoja? Onnistuuko Suomi säilyttämään ulkopoliittisen uskottavuutensa kotimaisen ja kansainvälisen yhteisön silmissä? Näitä kysymyksiä ruoditaan The Ulkopolitistin syyskauden kolmannessa jaksossa. Mukana keskustelemassa ovat humanitaarisen työn asiantuntija Merit Hietanen sekä Tampereen yliopiston tutkijatohtori Tiina Järvi.

title: As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three | Steve Bloomfield
content:
We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise

In the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world.

In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal.

title: How English Heritage Used Poetry to Engage Young People: Lessons for Museums
content:
Museum and heritage learning teams share a common challenge: how do you help young people make a personal connection with collections and historic places, rather than simply visiting them?

English Heritage tested one answer through Inspiring Voices, inviting young people aged 11 to 25 to respond to its sites through poetry, in written, spoken, filmed and visual forms. At a MuseumNext presentation, Laura Taylor, Digital Learning Manager at English Heritage, and Domi Blackmore, Learning and Participation Programmes Manager at English Heritage, shared how the work was designed and delivered, and what they learned.

According to the speakers, eight on-site workshops reached 119 young people against a target of 50, and an online poetry festival received 168 submissions against a target of 50. These figures measure participation and reach. The team also gathered immediate before-and-after feedback, but the presentation did not report longer-term measures of connection or wellbeing.

What museum teams can learn

  • Frame it as a creative response, not “poetry”. The word can deter bookings; a broader framing widened interest.

title: In Brazil’s elections, big techs’ transparency and cooperation policies translate as governance washing, according to this expert
content:
Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University NetLab has been following closely how this election unfolds on social media

Originally published on Global Voices

Art by Global Voices, created in Canva Pro.

Amid a series of corruption scandals, the 2026 general election in Brazil is also flooded with headlines about social media companies’ role in the campaign. Users supporting the candidacy of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the incumbent center-left candidate running for re-election, have been reporting a sudden drop in their Instagram Stories views when posting about politics. They say that Meta AI refused to generate images featuring Lula’s name and party number, while delivering the same request for Flávio Bolsonaro, his far-right opponent and the son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro.

On October 16, Meta admitted technical problems on its platforms which affected how pro-Lula content was delivered to users. As reported by the Associated Press, despite acknowledging “global technical glitches, strict anti-fraud measures, and regulatory compliance rather than targeted suppression,” the company that owns Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook denied any political bias.

title: Inside the cyber flaw scramble that brought the AI threat to life
content:
The exposure was immense, with AI multiplying the risks — and yet time-tested global cybersecurity procedures appeared to be functioning. Then suddenly, it all broke down.        

The decision by a cybersecurity company on Wednesday to prematurely release information about a flaw in the popular PHP computer programming language left much of the web exposed to hackers, triggering a panic that brought to life months of warnings of how the AI-powered era could cause widespread damage.

The flaws in PHP, discovered using AI tools through a months-long process coordinated by OpenAI, caused cyber agencies across Europe, the U.S., the U.K., Australia and Canada to post urgent warnings Wednesday. Numerous governments took websites offline as a precaution.

While no major hacking damage was immediately apparent, the way the incident unfolded over 72 hours showed how easily cybersecurity processes can break down and the outsized consequences of cyber risks in the AI era.

title: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle
content:
The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back

Dale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels.

The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labour politicians as a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”.

title: The Giant Scarf Project: How Creative Making Builds Community Engagement in Museums
content:
What happens when a football museum asks a city to knit? For the National Football Museum, the answer was a scarf more than 200 metres long, made from over 1,000 segments – and a way back into a community it had become distant from.

The Giant Scarf Project ran for two years in Preston, in partnership with Preston North End Community and Education Trust. It invited football lovers and loathers, experienced knitters and complete beginners to contribute a piece of a giant bar scarf. It was designed to reach people who might not see themselves reflected in a football museum, and to reconnect the museum with the city it left in 2012.

This case study sets out how the project was delivered, what it achieved, where the team had to adapt, and four lessons for museums planning community participation projects.

The National Football Museum opened in 2001 at Deepdale, home of Preston North End. Financial pressures led it to move to Manchester in 2012, but its Research and Archive Centre has remained at Deepdale ever since.

title: How to Turn an Archive into a Community Movement: Crowdsourcing Lessons from National Library of Wales
content:
Starting in autumn 2023, around 400 volunteers transcribed the names and addresses on the 390,296 signatures of the Welsh Women’s Peace Petition of 1923–24. Most of the work was done in about 15 months.

Their effort turned a document forgotten for nearly a century into a searchable record. That record then became the starting point for a nationwide movement of discovery, creativity and connection.

Dafydd Tudur, Head of Engagement at the National Library of Wales, felt that connection first-hand. Searching the newly digitised petition, he found his great-grandmother, Selina Edwards. She had signed in the hope that her newborn daughter, Gwenllian, might grow up in a world without war.

Volunteers uncovered other voices too. Jane Florence White, a mother from Cardiff, wrote a few words beside her name to explain why she signed: “One son killed, one lost his leg, one in lunatic asylum.” Another signatory wrote simply: “No more war.” Those notes had probably gone unread since the 1920s.

title: Chart: A record two-thirds of car sales in China are now electric vehicles
content:
• NEV record
  • Impact of Hormuz
  • NEV demand down 
  • Exports surge

    • For the first time, new-energy vehicles (NEVs) made up 67% of new car sales in China in September, according to the latest data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA).

    The figures show that NEVs, which include battery electric cars and plug-in hybrids, captured a record share of sales, even though fewer were sold than last year.

    This is because sales of combustion-engine cars are falling steeply, a trend that the CPCA has attributed to rising petrol prices following the start of the Hormuz crisis.

    Indeed, sales of fuel-only cars were down 31% year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, with plug-in hybrid sales down 26% – whereas battery EV sales were only down 4%.

    One analyst tells Carbon Brief that China’s rapidly growing EV fleet has offset demand for 143m barrels of oil since the start of the Hormuz crisis.

    Another says that the crisis is “reinforcing China’s electrification of road transport”.

    Meanwhile, amid slowing domestic sales, Chinese carmakers’ exports of NEVs more than doubled [in 2026 to date / in September] from a year earlier.

title: "Dying in Detention": Al Jazeera Investigates Immigrant Deaths in California's Adelanto ICE Jail
content:
At least 59 people have died in ICE custody since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, the highest number in more than a decade. Many deaths have been linked to medical neglect, including four of five recent deaths at California’s Adelanto Processing Center, according to a 2026 report by the state attorney general. Al Jazeera English’s Fault Lines investigated deaths at the facility, which is operated by the private prison company GEO Group, in the new documentary Dying in Detention.

“GEO Group has made over a billion dollars in profits from immigration detention. They have given more than a million dollars … to help reelect Donald Trump,” says correspondent Natasha Del Toro. “That raises a lot of questions for us about the relationship between GEO and the federal government, and some of these conflicts of interest.”

title: ECCCH-ACCESS Project Kick-off in Ankara
content:
Held in Ankara on the 2nd October 2026, the ECCCH-ACCESS Project Kick-Off introduced the project’s aim to connect cultural heritage institutions in Turkey (Türkiye) with the European Collaborative Cloud for Cultural Heritage (ECCCH) ecosystem.

Coordinated by Koç University Suna Kıraç Library and KARMA Lab, in partnership with MÜZEDER, Europa Nostra Türkiye, and Ankara AKS, the event featured presentations introducing the ECHOES consortium and the ECCCH approach, followed by a panel exploring experiences and practices in cultural heritage digitisation in Turkey.

The ECCCH process

ECCCH-ACCESS combines four complementary components:

  • awareness and community expansion through webinars and outreach activities;
  • sector mapping and feedback collection through surveys and moderated discussions;
  • knowledge translation through a dedicated website, multilingual training materials, and
  • AI-assisted dissemination; and participatory engagement through hackathons and co-design sessions.

    • Activities will engage museums, archaeological projects, libraries, researchers, and heritage professionals across Turkey through established institutional and professional networks.

title: The Vulnerability Apocalypse and Why We Should Fund Open Source
content:
If you use the internet at all, you may have noticed that a large percentage of sites suddenly went down earlier this week—and all your nerdiest friends were talking about "The Vulnerability Apocalypse” and this thing called PHP that powers nearly 70% of the websites on the internet. You may find yourself wondering: what is PHP, what just happened, what is the vulnerability apocalypse, and what do I need to do?  

To find out what you can personally do read the first blog post in this series!  

PHP is a programming language used mainly to create interactive websites. Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. But because it is open-source, maintenance of these critical systems depends on a small number of volunteers working on this in their free time. The disaster scenario that happened this past week is the perfect example of why we need more money and people supporting open-source projects. Corporations should be contributing both.

title: Amnesty: Uudet tiedot Sudanin Al-Faširista paljastavat ihmisten elävän kidutuksen, nälän ja pelon keskellä
content:
Maailman johtajat eivät ole onnistuneet puuttumaan Al-Faširin asukkaiden epätoivoiseen tilanteeseen sen jälkeen, kun sisällissodan osapuolena taistelevat puolisotilaalliset RSF-joukot valtasivat kaupungin väkivaltaisesti lokakuussa 2025. Humanitaaristen järjestöjen mukaan kaupungissa asuu nykyisin alle 70 000 ihmistä, kun ennen sotaa asukkaita oli yli miljoona.

Amnestyn haastattelemat ihmiset, jotka selviytyivät kaupungin verisestä valtaamisesta, kuvaavat Al-Faširia täysin tuhoutuneeksi: julkinen infrastruktuuri, viranomaisrakennukset ja sairaalat ovat raunioina. Humanitaarisen avun pääsy kaupunkiin on erittäin rajallista. RSF valvoo jatkuvasti sekä avustustyöntekijöitä että siviilejä.

”RSF-joukot väittävät, että Al-Faširiin on turvallista palata kaupungissa tapahtuneiden hirvittävien joukkomurhien jälkeen. Todellisuus on kuitenkin täysin toinen”, toteaa Amnestyn pääsihteeri Agnès Callamard.

title: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, children with Down syndrome are using a video game to safely navigate the internet
content:
A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game

Originally published on Global Voices

SafeClick is a video game that teaches children with Down syndrome about digital safety. A virtual assistant, Sol the Owl, that guides them through the game. Image by the game's developers, used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. 

Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web. This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ concerns about digital safety and the risks of being online.

Hän kertoo, mitä kansalliskielistrategia sanoo kielellisistä oikeuksista ja kieli-ilmastosta ja miksi uskallus on tärkeämpää kuin kielioppi. Mukana nähdään näytteitä larsmolaisen Otto Svarvarin Instagram-videoista, joissa hän puhuu iloisesti sekaisin suomea, ruotsia ja englantia. title: Unifying the Field: Library Advocacy From Greece to Europe
content:
Blog post by Giorgos Glossiotis

The Knowledge Rights 21 (KR21) Let Libraries Be Libraries Action Plan sets out nine asks for EU and national governments, covering licensing terms, contract override, digital locks, out-of-commerce works and education. Pursuing them at the national level takes coalitions, evidence and library associations confident enough to take copyright issues to national policymakers. Two days in Greece on 24 and 25 September focused on building that capacity, around the mid-term meeting of the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA) Europe Regional Division Committee (ERDC).

Day one, 24 September, featured two workshops for ERDC members and guests from the Greek library community, focused on KR21’s initiatives to support libraries in the 21st century. The sessions were led by KR21 representatives Stephen Wyber (Programme Lead/IFLA), Maarten Zeinstra (national coordinator for the Netherlands), and Giorgos Glossiotis (national coordinator for Greece and Cyprus).

title: Energiakriisi on vienyt Kuuban koulut uuteen normaaliin: Ei koulupukupakkoa eikä aina kirjojakaan
content:
Kun kuubalainen koululainen lähtee aamulla kouluun, hänen ei enää tarvitse pukea koulupukua.

”Lukuvuoden alussa kerrottiin, että tänä vuonna säännöistä joustetaan. Jos kotona ei ole sähköä tai vettä eikä univormua saada pestyä, lapsen voi lähettää tunnille t-paidassa ja housuissa”, havannalainen äiti Jennifer Suárez kertoo.

Kuuban uusi lukuvuosi alkoi syyskuussa. Resurssi-, polttoaine- ja rahapula näkyvät koulujen arjessa. Oppilaisiin kohdistuvia vaatimuksia on siksi höllennetty ja opetusta mukautettu olosuhteisiin.

Suárezin tytär aloitti alakoulun toisen luokan. Hän saa opetusta kaikissa tarvittavissa oppiaineissa niihin koulutetuilta opettajilta, mikä ei ole Kuubassa nykyisin itsestään selvää.

Opetusministeri Naima Trujillon mukaan lukuvuoden alkaessa maan 135 000 opettajan tehtävistä oli täytetty vain 73 prosenttia.

Opettajia on jo vuosien ajan lähtenyt ulkomaille tai siirtynyt muille aloille matalien palkkojen vuoksi. Opettajapula vaikuttaa noin 1,4 miljoonan lapsen ja nuoren koulunkäyntiin.

title: Noema’s AI Reading List
content:
AI’s climb up the capability ladder is moving more rapidly, even exponentially, than its progenitors expected. To keep up and put it in perspective, Noema has compiled a reading list of our best essays and interviews from a couple of years ago through the present. No doubt, we will need a new list again a few months down the road.

For now, here is a resource for following the trajectory of the most important technological breakthrough of this century so far.

1. How To Future-Proof Your Career In The Age Of AI

The most prized workers will be those who can decode a sea of outputs, spot the meaningful signal and translate it into action that others understand and trust.

by Nils Gilman

2. Whose AI Will Rule The World

As AI changes everything, the Chinese seem more optimistic than the Americans. Why?

by Jacob Dreyer

3. How AI Will Change Us

When the most patient, well-read, emotionally responsive conversationalist in the world is always available, what will we still need from one another?

by Houda Nait El Barj

4. AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class

AI doesn’t have to be a job destroyer. It offers us the opportunity to extend expertise to a larger set of workers.

by David Autor

title: Cyprus Parliament Reviews Reports on Abramovich-Linked Asset Transfers
content:
The Cypriot Parliament this week discussed recent revelations about corporate maneuvers that allowed firms ultimately owned by Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich to sidestep tax and transparency requirements.

The parliamentary hearings followed an investigation last week by OCCRP, CIReN, BBC, and TBIJ. The reports detailed how the Cyprus affiliate of multinational accountancy firm Deloitte, and corporate service provider MeritServus, worked together to backdate documents relating to companies beneficially owned by Abramovich. 

Doing so helped the companies retroactively transfer billions of dollars in assets from Cyprus to the British Virgin Islands, where they would not be subject to Cypriot laws on tax and public disclosure. 

OCCRP reached out to Deloitte’s offices in Cyprus and internationally for comment on the parliamentary hearing, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. Deloitte Cyprus previously told OCCRP it "acts in compliance with applicable laws."

MeritServus has been dissolved and it was not possible to obtain a comment.

title: Watch Rome Rise, Fall, and Rise Again in a Three-Minute 3D Timelapse
content:
Scholars disagree on when, exactly, Rome fell. But if you watch the new video from City 3D Timelapse above, you’ll understand the lack of debate on the question of whether it fell. Around the turn of the sixth century AD, buildings start vanishing at a rate that soon turns alarming; long before the end of the first millennium, it’s clear that Rome has been plunged into very hard times indeed. In the video’s accelerated visual history, that much-scrutinized 500-year span passes in a little more than five seconds. Just one minute later, it has spread not just beyond the old city limits, but beyond the very frame of the aerial view, becoming the vast urbanized region we know today.

Legend has it that Rome was founded in 753 BC, when Romulus killed his twin brother Remus. As reflected by the video, archaeological evidence suggests that the area was settled earlier, though the traditional date of Rome’s founding roughly coincides with the emergence of what we know as the Roman Kingdom.

title: Presidentti Stubb: Suomella ja Mongolialla on paljon yhteistä
content:
Tasavallan presidentti Alexander Stubb isännöi Mongolian presidentti Ukhnaa Khurelsukhin työvierailua Suomeen perjantaina 23. lokakuuta 2026.

Presidentti Stubb ja presidentti Khurelsukh tapasivat Presidentinlinnassa, jossa he keskustelivat Suomen ja Mongolian kahdenvälisten suhteiden lisäksi alueellisista turvallisuuskysymyksistä ja monenvälisestä yhteistyöstä.

”Suomella ja Mongolialla on paljon yhteistä. Arvostamme molemmat demokratiaa ja vakautta. Olemme molemmat pieniä maita suurten naapureiden vieressä sekä monenvälisen järjestelmän ja YK:n tukijoita”, presidentti Stubb sanoi keskustelun alussa.

Presidentti Stubb kertoi myös ajankohtaisen päivityksen Euroopan turvallisuustilanteesta ja Venäjän hyökkäyssodasta Ukrainassa.

Vierailun aikana allekirjoitettiin neljä yhteisymmärryspöytäkirjaa. Suomi ja Mongolia tiivistävät yhteistyötä koulutuksen ja kulttuurin aloilla.

Iltapäivällä presidentit osallistuivat Suomen ja Mongolian väliseen yritystapahtumaan Säätytalolla. Yksi työvierailun tavoitteista oli vahvistaa Suomen ja Mongolian välistä kauppaa. Presidentti Khurelsukhin mukana oli lähes 70 henkilön kokoinen yritysvaltuuskunta.

title: After Millions in Stolen SNAP Benefits, Trump Administration Moves to Fight Theft
content:
The Trump administration this week announced an overhaul of the nation’s food stamp payment system, aimed at modernizing benefit cards to protect families from electronic theft. The move comes a week after ProPublica published an investigation showing how $470 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits were stolen from recipients last year alone, in large part because these cards are technologically outdated.

ProPublica’s story highlighted victims’ experiences and examined repeated failures by Congress and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to upgrade Electronic Benefits Transfer, or EBT, cards nationally. ProPublica’s reporting was shared around the department, according to two USDA officials.

title: PHP2Shell exposes the funding gap in open-source security
content:
On 21 October 2026, the PHP project released fixes for two critical security vulnerabilities, collectively known as PHP2Shell. Under certain conditions, these vulnerabilities could allow attackers to execute code on affected web servers without authentication.

PHP underpins a substantial share of the web, including public services, businesses, and widely used publishing platforms. The incident highlights a fundamental challenge in open-source security: finding vulnerabilities is only the first step. Fixing them, and preventing similar flaws in the future, requires sustained investment.

In 2024, the Sovereign Tech Agency commissioned the first external security audit of PHP’s core in over a decade, coordinated by OSTIF and conducted by Quarkslab. The audit identified 17 security-related findings and contributed to subsequent work on the underlying problem behind one of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. The organization explicitly recognized the value of this investment.

title: Unga skribenter värnar om sin egen röst i en tid av AI
content:
Wilhelmina Meyer från Gymnasiet Lärkan i Helsingfors vinner årets ”Argh? – kolumntävlingen för dig som har något på hjärtat”. I novelltävlingen ”Vad händer?” för årskurserna 7-9 tar Saga Saloviin från Winellska skolan i Kyrkslätt hem segern.

Kolumner och noveller är utmanande genrer. På Helsingfors bokmässa prisbelönas åtta unga som skriver med personlig närhet, samhällsengagemang och språklig säkerhet.

Under våren ordnade Svenska modersmålslärarföreningen i Finland (SMLF) två skrivtävlingar – en kolumntävling för studerande vid andra stadiet och en novelltävling för elever i årskurserna 7-9.

Många av bidragen i årets kolumntävling Argh? handlar om hur AI och algoritmer påverkar samhället. Samtidigt ser juryn en tydlig vilja hos skribenterna att tänka självständigt och skriva med en egen röst.

Psykisk ohälsa är ett tema som återkommer år efter år. I årets texter kommer temat nära, med skildringar av både egna och närståendes erfarenheter.

I novelltävlingen Vad händer? ser juryn en gemensam nämnare: det märks att skribenterna är vana läsare. De vet hur både intrig och språk driver en berättelse framåt och håller läsarens intresse vid liv.

title: Top ICC official urges EU to act ‘as soon as possible’ on US sanctions
content:
THE HAGUE — The European Commission should act “as soon as possible” to give clear guidance on U.S. sanctions against the International Criminal Court, its top administrative official told POLITICO in an interview.

Osvaldo Zavala Giler, who oversees the day-to-day functioning of the Hague-based court as the institution’s registrar, said his job became “preparing for sanctions” as the White House imposed an escalating regime of restrictions against it.

The Trump administration targeted prosecutors and judges from the court first in February 2025 before announcing blanket sanctions on Oct. 9 this year. The EU has repeatedly backed the Court against Washington, but it has resisted calls to activate a mechanism that would forbid firms from complying with U.S. laws.

That has agonized senior figures in The Hague. Zavala Giler said the Commission’s “lack of clarity” left private companies and NGOs in the dark over whether they should comply with sanctions decided by Washington — and what risks they face if they don’t.

title: US midterms: what a new Congress could – and could not – change for Europe
content:
US midterm elections traditionally attract fewer voters than presidential contests. But this year’s vote is drawing considerable attention at home and abroad, especially in Europe.

Europe has not even needed to wait for the election results to feel their impact. With fuel prices weighing on American voters, Donald Trump has recently reached a deal to start importing Russian diesel in the hope of lowering fuel prices before election day. It was a stunning reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.

The contrast with Europe is striking. On October 12, the EU adopted its largest single expansion of sanctions against Russia’s military-industrial complex, targeting 1,569 individuals and entities. Four days later, Trump waived major new US sanctions on Russia, under legislation he had signed just a few weeks before.

These decisions send an uncomfortable message to Kyiv and European capitals: pressure on Russia is not a given, and can be relaxed when US electoral interests take priority.

With Republican losses looking increasingly likely, US Congress could look very different in a few weeks. But could a new Congress change US-Europe relations?
snippet: US midterm elections traditionally attract fewer voters than presidential contests. But this year’s vote is drawing considerable attention at home and abroad, especially in Europe.

title: Unlocking the secrets of the ‘Dragon Man’ skull – and what it reveals about human evolution
content:
In September 2018, China Daily ran a story that found its way to my desk. It featured the photograph of a beautifully preserved fossil skull with huge brow-ridges, with a caption speculating – wrongly, as it would turn out – that it belonged to a species of human known as Homo heidelbergensis.

The article told a remarkable story about the discovery of this fossil some 85 years earlier. Japanese forces had been occupying the city of Harbin in north-eastern China in 1933. They ordered a team of local workers to help build a railway bridge across the Songhua River.

The workers uncovered the skull in river deposits, and one of them hid it from the Japanese by lowering it down a disused well. Feeling ashamed of having worked for the enemy, he kept quiet about the find for many years. Finally some 80 years later he told his son and grandson as he lay dying, which led to the almost intact skull being recovered and later donated to Hebei Geo University near Beijing.

title: The Nordic-Baltic Eight policy brief: China’s green statecraft and NB8 Arctic security
content:
New publication in the NB8 policy brief series by Dana Dūda (LIIA), Konstantinas Andrijauskas (IIRPS VU) and Björn Cappelin (UI).

Energy dependence has become a geopolitical liability. Russia’s war against Ukraine, the US-Iran war and tensions with the Kingdom of Denmark over Greenland have all exposed the strategic weight of energy independence, critical minerals, and Arctic access. For the eight Nordic-Baltic states (NB8), the next vulnerability may emerge from the green transition itself, where China’s dominance in clean technologies and critical mineral processing can be converted into strategic leverage. Some dependence is unavoidable in the short term; the task is to manage it deliberately rather than let it accumulate by default. This policy brief argues for integrating green energy security and Arctic security within a one strategic framework, because the Arctic’s critical mineral resources, renewable energy infrastructure and emerging transport and digital connectivity projects are relevant to Europe’s efforts to strengthen its energy dependence. This brief proposes collective measures to limit strategic dependence on China in the long term.
